item.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Dependent on Fossil Fuels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: comprehensive analysis with clear reporting and useful vocabulary

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India and southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño, the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.…

item.title: Elders in Bali renew push against new offshore gas terminal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: local issue with global implications, well-reported

- Plans to build a floating LNG storage facility off eastern Bali continue to attract opposition from affected communities on the Indonesian island.

- Civil society organizations have also criticized the planned development, pointing to tandem plans to develop vast solar energy capacity that have yet to be advanced.

- Local officials argue that higher demand for electricity necessitates building infrastructure to ensure reliable electricity, but campaigners say this will lock in greenhouse gas emissions in conflict with marketing efforts to portray the island as a green holiday destination.

DENPASAR, Indonesia — Customary leaders from Serangan village in Bali have renewed local opposition to a planned liquefied natural gas terminal off the east coast of the Indonesian island, saying the floating LNG site is too close to customary fishing grounds.

“We disagree with the 3.5-kilometer distance [2.2 miles] because the vessel is large, and very close to the village’s sacred point as well as our fishing routes,” said I Nyoman Gede Pariartha, the traditional leader in Serangan, at a meeting on Nov. 14.

Earlier this year Indonesia’s environment ministry issued an environmental permit for a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) off the eastern coast of Serangan island in Bali. The new infrastructure is intended to improve the reliability of Bali’s electricity supply by supplying gas-fired power plants amid rising electricity demand on the island.

Bali has a population of 4.5 million, but the island received almost 7 million tourism visits in 2025 and, since the pandemic, has increasingly been host to longer-term visitors.

Increasing electricity demand on the island is supplied by several power plants on Bali, including the gas-fired Pesanggaran power station, a 200 megawatt capacity facility next to a protected mangrove forest on the northern fringe of Benoa Bay.

In addition, up to 30% of the island’s electricity is supplied by cables from neighboring Java, the world’s most populous island.

The planned new FSRU site east of Bali will receive liquified natural gas offshore from tankers, and convert the fuel back into natural gas before supplying it through pipelines to Pesanggaran power station.

However, the new FSRU location has previously been moved from another site in Sidakarya village amid local opposition in an area with a history of grassroots resistance to large-scale development.

In 2013, a proposal backed by an oligarch to reclaim hundreds of hectares of the bay for luxury resorts, hotels and entertainment facilities met with opposition.

Artists, civil society, customary village leaders and students coalesced under a broad movement to protect Benoa Bay’s mangroves, marine ecosystems, livelihoods and sacred sites. The proposal was eventually shelved after years of campaigning.

Greenpeace action

Greenpeace activists floated a banner in Benoa Bay in the shape of a sea turtle saying “No Fossil Gas in Paradise” ahead of COP31 in Turkey, which ended on Nov. 22 without a new agreement on fossil fuels to prevent breakdown of global climate.

“We are witnessing how the climate crisis is fueling disasters that are intensifying and worsening year after year,” said Iqbal Damanik, climate and energy manager at Greenpeace Indonesia. “All of these climate-related disasters are driven by the use of fossil fuels.”

“Adding LNG facilities in southern Bali will shrink fishing grounds, destroy mangrove ecosystems, and harm sea turtle habitats,” said Greenpeace Indonesia lead Yuyun Harmono. “Stop using fossil gas and shift focus immediately to renewables.”

Indonesia is struggling to overcome structural limitations to the energy transition due to a surplus of independent coal producers given lucrative take-or-pay contracts to supply the Java-Bali grid, which serves a majority of the population in the world’s fourth-largest country.

In effect, coal plants are paid to burn coal whether or not Indonesia’s national grid, PLN, buys the electricity.

The Institute Essential Services Reform, a think tank focused on energy, estimates total solar energy potential in Bali of up to 22 gigawatts, which is greater than the total installed capacity from all sources on Denmark’s national grid.

In 2025, Bali governor I Wayan Koster unveiled a new rooftop solar energy plan to help Bali achieve net zero emission by 2045, a target the governor announced in 2023. The government in Bali could not be reached for comment.

“Adding new fossil-fuel capacity will only prolong Indonesia’s entrapment in a fossil-fuel-dependent system and hinder the energy transition,” Yuyun said.

Banner image: A banner opposing the use of gas for power generation in Bali. Image by Luh De Suriyani/Mongabay Indonesia.

This story was first published here in Indonesian on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.title: Indonesian Borneo’s forests go quiet as smoke silences gibbons. Their singing matters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique perspective on environmental impact with clear detail

- Researchers in Indonesian Borneo have observed that gibbons’ morning songs have been reduced or absent during this fire season, a pattern also observed during previous fires.

- Researchers have not yet formally analyzed their findings, but suspect a major driver is smoke, which irritates gibbons’ airways and reduces the light that cues morning duets.

- Longer term, researchers fear gibbons’ health and fertility will be reduced by habitat disturbances and loss of food caused by the fires.

- When gibbons sing less, it also complicates the work of researchers, who typically rely on monitoring songs to find and count the animals.

Around dawn, a gibbon pair starts to sing. Their voices interweave, and the duet builds to a crescendo that fills the canopy. Across much of the Bornean forest, this is the sound of the morning.

But since smoke from Indonesia’s worst fire crisis in over a decade has engulfed the island, forests have become noticeably quieter. On days when the haze is thick, the Borneo Nature Foundation (BNF) field team in Sebangau, Central Kalimantan, reports that gibbons sing less. Their songs sound shorter. Morning duets start later than usual, if they happen at all.

Susan Cheyne, BNF’s co-director and vice-chair of the IUCN Primate Specialist Group Section on Small Apes, documented a similar pattern following forest fires in the same area in 2006.

Researchers have yet to formally analyze their observations of the effects of this year’s fires, and will not be able to separate the different factors until the fires have subsided and fieldwork can resume. Cheyne believes several causes may be at play, with smoke — which irritates gibbons’ airways and reduces the light that cues morning duets — as a major driver.

Why gibbon song matters

Singing plays a central role in the social and reproductive lives of gibbons. Fiercely territorial, socially monogamous primates, they sing not only to attract mates, but also to defend their territory. Paired adults perform elaborate duets to demonstrate the strength of their bond and ward off neighboring groups. Their songs are remarkably sophisticated, following rhythmic patterns and note sequences in ways that primatologists have compared to human music and language.

For gibbons, singing demands considerable energy and coordination — it is “an honest signal biologically,” according to Cheyne. A complex, well synchronized duet is difficult to fake, serving as a reliable sign of a healthy, strongly bonded pair.

Gibbon vocal behavior is also sensitive to environmental conditions. Research has found that they appear to sing less when exposed to disturbances like rain and noise pollution.

How smoke disrupts morning duets

Since mid-September, air quality in Central Kalimantan, has frequently reached hazardous levels. In the capital, Palangkaraya, pollution levels in October peaked at 11,981, nearly four times the level the U.S. Air Quality Index classifies as hazardous. As of Nov. 2, the Indonesian Ministry of Health reported more than 400,000 cases of acute respiratory infections across Central Kalimantan and six other affected provinces.

Borneo is home to four species of gibbons, all of which are endemic and endangered. Like humans, they have been exposed to high concentrations of smoke particles. Cheyne expects the smoke to affect gibbons in similar ways, irritating their airways and making it harder to breathe. This is likely one of the driving factors behind the drop in singing.

“I’m sure an opera singer would never be able to hit the notes and range and frequency that they should be able to if they’re constantly breathing in smoke,” she says.

Smoke may also affect singing by reducing visibility and dimming the light inside the forest. An analysis of more than 300 days of gibbon singing data from northern Lao PDR found gibbons tend to sing later and less often on foggy mornings. Gibbons typically perform their duets around sunrise, as light starts to filter through the canopy.

“We think that light is the main cue,” Cheyne says. When haze obscures sunrise, gibbons may delay their singing or skip it altogether.

According to Cheyne, there is also a visual, acrobatic component to their territorial displays, which may help explain later starts on hazy days. “They’re not just sitting; they’re swinging and singing at the same time.”

Alasdair Owens, a post-graduate researcher at the University of Exeter in England who uses passive acoustic data to study Bornean white-bearded gibbons (Hylobates albibarbis), says a factor that may become more evident in coming months is the lasting effect of the fires on the availability of fruit, which makes up the bulk of gibbon diets. Food shortages, he says, could impact their singing.

Fires have burned across parts of the ranges of Borneo’s gibbons, including an estimated 13,000 hectares (32,100 acres) inside Sebangau National Park. Previous El Niño fires have led to what Owens describes as “almost famine conditions” in the forest.

A 2015 study on orangutans, gibbons’ larger relatives, found that females adjusted their behavior for months following forest fires and fruit shortages. They rested more and traveled less to reduce energy expenditure. Gibbons have also been found to sing less when food availability declines.

The longer-term effects of reduced singing on gibbons’ health, social relationships and reproductive success remain unclear. Cheyne predicts that if families sing less, neighbors might encroach on their territory, leading to conflict between groups, while young gibbons may struggle to find mates.

Disruptions to gibbons’ daily routines caused by haze and delayed morning duets could also have far-reaching consequences. If gibbons reduce their active hours, they may have less time to feed and socialize, Cheyne says.

How to count silent gibbons…

item.title: Timor-Leste issues guidelines for whale-watching, but malpractice is rife as industry booms
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting case study with clear reporting

- Timor-Leste’s booming swim-with-whales tourism industry is seeing growing numbers of operators and increasingly aggressive practices, raising concerns about its impact on migrating pygmy blue whales.

- New official guidelines aim to protect whales, but repeated breaches have exposed the lack of enforcement in an industry with no formal regulatory framework —the government is aiming for regulations to be legally reviewed by next year.

- Disagreements between operators and scientists over how closely tourists can approach whales highlight the challenges of balancing commercial interests with animal welfare.

- Conservationists and operators want licensing, monitoring and limits on boat numbers, and greater participation from Timorese in an industry dominated by foreign firms.

DILI, Timor-Leste — As the annual whale migration gets into full swing in Timor-Leste, conservationists are raising concerns about increasingly aggressive tourist encounters with the world’s largest animals, despite new guidelines designed to protect them.

Whale tourism is booming in a country whose waters are known as a “superhighway” for marine mammals. Migrating pygmy blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus brevicauda) are the star attraction for tourists seeking the experience of a lifetime.

Though haze from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia made spotting whale spouts difficult in the earlier part of the season, industry-watchers have noticed a marked increase in the number of operators on the water this year.

By the end of October, however, fewer whales had passed through the Ombai-Wetar Strait, which lies off the northern coast of Timor-Leste. This is likely because El Niño and the positive Indian Ocean Dipole have brought cooler waters in the region, delaying the migration of the whales, says cetacean ecologist Professor Karen Edyvane, who, in the past decade, has monitored migrating pygmy blue whales in Timor-Leste’s waters.

This has meant more intense competition among whale tour operators to deliver experiences for customers, who pay $250-350 a day for the chance to swim with one of the few hundred pygmy blue whales that pass through each year.

Industry-watchers have noticed cowboyish practices in the busiest season yet. Boats cutting across whales’ paths, operators pursuing mothers with calves, too many swimmers in the water at once — one tourist was taken out to swim with a whale on a jet ski — are among the reported violations.

“We’ve seen the same bad behavior as in the last few years — just more of it with the new boats,” Tom Quinney, a photographer who on Nov. 12 documented nine boats chasing what was believed to be a pregnant whale off the coast of Dili, told Mongabay in a written message. Quinney’s drone footage captures tourists free-diving with the whale, swimming within a few meters of it, and another drone being flown just above its head.

These practices breach guidelines released on Sept. 30 by the Timorese government and nonprofit Conservation International, with assistance from the Australian government and technical input from whale experts, including Edyvane.

Swimming with whales can be conducted responsibly if science and evidence-based guidelines are followed, but poorly managed encounters can have serious consequences for the cetaceans, Edyvane says.

Disruptions from boats and swimmers posing for Instagram photographs can cause pygmy blue whales to expend energy that they need to complete their annual migration from Indonesia’s Banda Sea, through Timor-Leste, to Australia.

“Critically, many of the animals we see in Timor-Leste’s waters are nursing mothers and calves – animals which need to nurse and rest, without ongoing disturbance from tour boats,” Edyvane told Mongabay in a written message.

From her whale monitoring field research station in Subaun on Timor-Leste’s northern coast, Edyvane has documented pygmy blue whales that are underweight, with their ribs and vertebrae visible. She suspects ocean warming is disrupting the upwellings that sustain their food supply.

Whale tourism could provide a significant boost to Timor-Leste’s nascent tourism economy. But the industry will have no future if it disrupts the migration on which it depends, says Delio da Costa, project coordinator for the Solutions for Marine and Coastal Resilience in the Coral Triangle (SOMACORE) at Conservation International.

Da Costa was part of the team that developed the new guidelines, which are an expanded version of recommendations published in 2020. They establish rules for approaching whales, including minimum distances and speed limits, and prohibit operators from chasing animals or blocking their paths.

Monitoring the ‘sinners’

Despite repeated reports of breaches, there have been no apparent consequences for rogue operators. Timor-Leste lacks a formal regulatory framework for whale tourism, and no operator has been apprehended for misconduct in the decade since the industry emerged.

It also lacks a clear avenue for complaints, which are directed instead to a general tourism information phone number and email. The government says it has yet to receive any whale-related complaints through these channels.

But observers are increasingly calling out malpractice. Last December, toward the end of the 2025 season, photographer Ollie Clarke wrote an open letter to the industry after witnessing multiple operators flouting internationally recognized rules. He described a “race to the bottom” as new players flood the market.

Also in December 2025, Quinney documented six boats pursuing a mother pygmy blue whale and her calf off the coast of the city of Manatuto.

One of the most serious breaches this year involved a boat speeding into the path of a female pygmy blue whale and her calf. Drone footage taken by marine biologist Ywen Mieybégué, seen by Mongabay, identified the vessel as belonging to Timor Sunshine Divers, one of the country’s largest operators.…

item.title: Analysis: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: analysis of a complex issue with useful context

NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. Still, the outcome was even worse than expected—a failure to reach an overall agreement at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by climate change. While negotiations collapsed over one main point of contention—whether to include language about fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming—this fight over this has been building for many years. During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn’t a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they voiced their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately got in line. This time, many countries were not willing to do that.

By Peter Prengaman, Associated Press

item.title: Bush dogs are very rare. You’re 100x more likely to see a jaguar
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique subject matter, but less detailed reporting

Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.

Biologists can spend decades working in the Amazon without seeing a bush dog. A new study quantifies just how rare the wild canids are.

Writing in Canid Biology & Conservation, Robert Wallace and his colleagues at the Wildlife Conservation Society analyzed 25 years of camera-trap data from 97 sites across seven South American countries. In more than 2.1 million photographs, taken over 611,159 camera-trap nights, bush dogs (Speothos venaticus) appeared on just 12 occasions.

Jaguars (Panthera onca) turned up about 100 times as often, and ocelots nearly 280 times. Even the short-eared dog (Atelocynus microtis), so fleetingly rare that it’s been nicknamed the “ghost dog,” was recorded 50 times as often as the bush dog.

Bush dogs are found from Costa Rica to northeastern Argentina. They have short legs, weigh up to 7 kilograms (about 15 pounds), and sometimes hunt in packs of a dozen. In Brazil’s Cerrado, a single family group was found to occupy a home range of 140 square kilometers (54 square miles).

In the latest study, the researchers analyzed footage from cameras mostly set 40–50 centimeters (16-20 inches) above the ground to photograph jaguars, which may have been a little high for bush dogs. Yet they readily photographed pacas, rodents of much the same size and shape as bush dogs, on nearly 40,000 occasions. A pack of dogs should also be easier to photograph than a solitary animal.

The researchers estimate that there are well under one bush dog per 100 km2 (roughly three per 100 mi2) across much of the species’ range. In the Amazon, the figure could be as low as one per 350 km2 (three per 350 mi2). Much of the data come from relatively intact forests in the western Amazon.

Living in packs makes bush dogs susceptible to outbreaks of disease. Domestic dogs brought into forests by hunters or settlers can carry canine distemper, parvovirus, and rabies. An entire pack could succumb to an infection picked up from a domestic dog.

The bush dog’s classification as near threatened on the IUCN Red List dates to 2011. The authors are calling for a reassessment.

Banner image: Scientists who work in the forests of Bolivia, Colombia, Brazil, and Ecuador have long known that seeing a bush dog is an extraordinary event. Image ©️ WCS.
